fields.claim_quote: since $a_{n_k}$ is bounded above (so that $\limsup _{k \rightarrow \infty} a_{n_k}$ is finite), it follows that $b_{n_{k_m}}$ converges to the difference
fields.complete_source:
Since the case when $\limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n=+\infty$ and $\limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty} b_n=-\infty$ has been excluded from consideration, we note that the inequality is obvious if $\limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n=+\infty$. Hence we shall assume that $\left\{a_n\right\}$ is bounded above.

Let $\left\{n_k\right\}$ be a subsequence of the positive integers such that $\lim _{k \rightarrow \infty}\left(a_{n_k}+\right.$ $\left.b_{n_k}\right)=\limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(a_n+b_n\right)$. Then choose a subsequence of the positive integers $\left\{k_m\right\}$ such that
$$
\lim _{m \rightarrow \infty} a_{n_{k_m}}=\limsup _{k \rightarrow \infty} a_{n_k} .
$$
The subsequence $a_{n_{k_m}}+b_{n_{k_m}}$ still converges to the same limit as $a_{n_k}+b_{n_k}$, i.e., to $\limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(a_n+b_n\right)$. Hence, since $a_{n_k}$ is bounded above (so that $\limsup _{k \rightarrow \infty} a_{n_k}$ is finite), it follows that $b_{n_{k_m}}$ converges to the difference
$$
\lim _{m \rightarrow \infty} b_{n_{k_m}}=\lim _{m \rightarrow \infty}\left(a_{n_{k_m}}+b_{n_{k_m}}\right)-\lim _{m \rightarrow \infty} a_{n_{k_m}} .
$$
Thus we have proved that there exist subsequences $\left\{a_{n_{k_m}}\right\}$ and $\left\{b_{n_{k_m}}\right\}$ which converge to limits $a$ and $b$ respectively such that $a+b=\limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(a_n+b_n^*\right)$. Since $a$ is the limit of a subsequence of $\left\{a_n\right\}$ and $b$ is the limit of a subsequence of $\left\{b_n\right\}$, it follows that $a \leq \limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n$ and $b \leq \limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty} b_n$, from which the desired inequality follows.
fields.explanation:
The claim excludes +∞ but fails to exclude divergence to -∞. A lower bound, or some separate hypothesis ensuring the limsup is greater than -∞, is also needed.

Full-context and formalization review: Original positive-index sequencea_n=−n with n_k=k is bounded above but has limsup−infinity. Completing the full source context withb_n=0 avoids the forbidden infinity-minus-infinity sum, and the identity subsequences realize the chosen limsups. Lean natural index0 represents sourceindex1, hence−(n+1). Reindexing by one preserves the exact original positive-index sequence. The limsup inequality itself is not refuted.
fields.flaw: Boundedness above of the selected subsequence implies that its limsup is finite, permitting subtraction of the two limits.
fields.problem:
For any two real sequences $\left\{a_{n}\right\},\left\{b_{n}\right\}$, prove that $\limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(a_{n}+b_{n}\right) \leq \limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty} a_{n}+\limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty} b_{n},$ provided the sum on the right is not of the form $\infty-\infty$.

DEFINITIONS / CONVENTIONS:
The sequences are real-valued. limsup is taken in the extended real line [-infty, +infty] (Rudin's definition: the supremum of the set of subsequential limits in the extended reals, equivalently lim_{n->infty} sup_{k>=n} a_k); so each limsup may be -infty or +infty. Extended-real addition follows the usual conventions (x + (+infty) = +infty for x > -infty, x + (-infty) = -infty for x < +infty), and the hypothesis excludes exactly the case where one limsup is +infty and the other is -infty.

fields.witness: Let n_k=k and a_n=-n. Then the selected subsequence is a_{n_k}=-k. It is bounded above: for every k≥1, -k≤-1. But limsup_{k→∞}(-k)=-∞, which is not finite as a real number. Thus boundedness above alone does not justify subtraction of ordinary finite limits. Complete the surrounding context with b_n=0 and identity subsequences n_k=k and k_m=m. Then limsup(a_n)=-infinity and limsup(b_n)=0, so the right-hand sum is -infinity+0 and satisfies the source's exclusion of infinity-minus-infinity.
